title: The Woman whose Hands were Cut Off

full_text:
In a city of the Levant lived a virtuous and charitable young woman whose devotion to helping the poor was known to all. One bitter winter day, a shivering beggar knocked at her door, starving and begging for a single morsel of bread in the name of the Creator. Having no bread baked, the maiden gave him two silver bracelets from her own arms, that he might purchase food and shelter.

However, her husband's envious sister observed the act and falsely accused the maiden before her brother, claiming she had squandered the household jewels on an impostor. In a fit of irrational fury, the suspicious husband drove the innocent maiden into the wilderness, where she suffered hardship and exposure.

Alone in the forest, the virtuous woman placed her trust in divine providence. She found shelter in an ancient hermitage where she tended sick animals and prayed for her family’s guidance.

Years passed, and a wealthy, just king of a neighboring realm, riding through the forest on a hunt, found the noble hermit woman. Struck by her saintly countenance and serene wisdom, the king inquired into her history. When she recounted her unjust suffering with neither bitterness nor desire for vengeance, the king’s heart was moved to profound reverence.

He brought her to his royal palace, treated her as his most honored guest, and ordered his judges to investigate the truth of her past.

The truth was brought to light: the envious sister-in-law, stricken with illness and remorse, confessed her wicked slander before the magistrates. The former husband, weeping in ashes and sackcloth, arrived at the court begging for forgiveness.

The noble woman harbored no wrath; she forgave her former husband and embraced her repentant sister-in-law, proving that patience and pure charity outlast the deepest winter of adversity and receive the highest rewards of peace.
moral: Divine justice and patient endurance overcome the darkest slanders and restore honor to the pure.
